sections.history: Erukkattampuliyur, the old name of the town now called Rajendrapattinam, lies in the Nadu Nadu country of the Cuddalore district, not far from Srimushnam. It is among the shrines praised in the Tevaram, and tradition holds that the child-saint Tirugnana Sambandar sang here, which marks it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The town's later name carries a Chola memory: it is said that the emperor Rajaraja Chola prayed at this temple for an heir and was blessed with a son, Rajendra, who in turn enlarged and endowed the shrine, so that the place came to be called Rajendrapattinam. The temple is also honoured as the birthplace of Tiru Neelakanta Yazhpanar, counted among the sixty-three Nayanmar saints. Raised in stone in the Chola centuries and renewed by later patrons, it has stayed in worship through the long life of the Tamil country.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered through a five-tiered rajagopuram, and though its earliest fabric is of Chola work its present form owes much to the later Nagarathar tradition of temple-keeping. Within, the sanctum holds the linga of Neelakandeswarar, the Lord of the blue throat, while the goddess Neelamalar Kanni is honoured in her own shrine. As one of the Puliyur temples the complex keeps the memory of the sage Vyaghrapada, and shrines to the Nayanar saints, to Murugan, and to the attendant deities stand within the enclosure. The whole keeps the ordered calm of a temple long cared for by a devout mercantile community.
sections.legends: The temple belongs to the group of Puliyur shrines — counted by some as the five Pancha Puliyur and by others among the nine Nava Puliyur — sanctified by the sage Vyaghrapada. In the well-loved story he was a devotee who gathered flowers before dawn for the worship of Shiva as the dancer of Chidambaram, and, that his hands and feet might not be torn by thorns and his eyes might see in the dark, the Lord granted him the feet and eyes of a tiger; from this he was called Vyaghrapada, the tiger-footed, and the Puliyur towns where he worshipped carry 'puli,' tiger, in their names. Woven into the temple's own memory is the Chola prayer for a son that gave Rajendrapattinam its name, and the birth here of the Nayanar Neelakanta Yazhpanar, the yazh-player whose steadfast devotion is sung among the sixty-three.
sections.festivals: As at every Shiva temple, Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are kept with devotion, and the Tamil month of Margazhi and the days of the sixty-three Nayanmar are observed with feeling, fitting for a shrine that is itself a saint's birthplace. The annual Brahmotsavam and the car festival draw the fullest gatherings. Dates follow the Tamil calendar and change each year, so confirm them locally before visiting.
sections.experience: Rajendrapattinam lies off the main pilgrim roads, and a visit here is unhurried and close to the land. Enter beneath the five-tiered gopuram, come before the linga of Neelakandeswarar, and turn to the goddess Neelamalar Kanni in her shrine. Devotees who know the Puliyur tradition pause at the memory of Vyaghrapada, and those who honour the Nayanmar come mindful that this is the birthplace of Neelakanta Yazhpanar. The temple keeps the quiet dignity of an old Chola foundation tended across the centuries.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Rajendrapattinam (Erukkattampuliyur) lies in the Virudhachalam region of the Cuddalore district, near the Virudhachalam–Jayamkondam road and close to Srimushnam. Virudhachalam, about 15 km away, is the nearest town and railhead; buses serve the village from there and from Srimushnam. The nearest airports are at Tiruchirappalli and Puducherry. Confirm the final approach locally.
